title: Marriage
hookLine: for some churches a sacrament, for others a covenant; all see it as faithful love

cards: Two people stand at the front of a church, hands joined, a little nervous. The words they repeat are old.

In the Book of Common Prayer, the groom promises: "to have and to hold from this day forward, for better for worse, for richer for poorer, in sickness and in health, to love and to cherish, till death us do part."
The bride's promise runs almost word for word the same. Nobody in the room knows which of those they'll get. That's the point.
They promise all of it, in advance. Christians in quite different churches make promises like these, even when they explain them in different words.

teach.b: The root is in the opening pages of Genesis: "Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh." Leave, cleave, become one.
When Jesus is asked about divorce, he goes straight back to that verse and adds a line still heard at weddings: "What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder."
So for him, marriage isn't only a private contract. God is the one joining. Here churches describe it differently.
Catholic and Orthodox Christians count marriage as a sacrament: a holy sign through which God's grace is truly given to the couple.
In the Catholic understanding, the bride and groom are the ministers of the sacrament to each other. Lutheran and Reformed churches don't number marriage among the sacraments.
They call it a covenant, or a holy estate that God created and blesses: a promise made before God and witnesses, with God as a party to it.
Paul, writing to the Ephesians about husbands and wives, says: "This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church." That one line holds the common ground.

Whatever word a church uses, sacrament or covenant, they agree that a faithful marriage is meant to show something about God: love that chooses the other person again, for better and for worse, and doesn't leave.

how: Christians marry in church services with vows exchanged before God and witnesses; Catholic and Orthodox churches celebrate marriage as a sacrament, while Protestant churches celebrate it as a covenant or holy estate blessed by God.

o: a faithful union: sacrament or covenant before God
a public party celebrating a couple in love
a legal contract that joins two families' property

s: every church calls marriage a sacrament
Catholic and Orthodox churches do; Lutheran and Reformed churches, among others, call it a covenant or holy estate.
in Catholic teaching, the couple are the ministers of the sacrament
the bride and groom give the sacrament to each other.
Jesus treats marriage as only a private contract
he says God does the joining: "what therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder."

games.q: people come to Jesus with a question about divorce. where does he go for his answer?
o: to the customs of his own day.
back to Genesis: the two shall be one flesh.
games.why: he goes back to the beginning, to Genesis 2:24, and adds: "what therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder."

practice: Choose a couple you know, your parents, grandparents, friends, neighbors, or your own marriage if you have one, and picture them on an ordinary day, not the wedding day: somebody's tired, somebody's doing dishes.
Which of the old vows are they living right now? If you pray, you can pray for them by name; if you don't, just wish them well, specifically.

wordCard.voice: Marriage. For Catholic and Orthodox Christians, a sacrament; for Lutheran and Reformed churches, among others, a covenant before God. For both, faithful love: two becoming one flesh.

carryVoice: Your line: two becoming one. For better, for worse, chosen again. Until tomorrow.
